title: Heaps of jewels (section 24)
hookLine: jewels piled high as mountains are less than keeping four lines

lines: A BAG LEFT ON A TRAIN.
cards: A woman leaves her bag on a train: wallet, phone, keys, the ring she took off to wash her hands. Gone. That night, unable to sleep, she finds herself saying a poem she learned as a girl, every line still there.
The train took everything she carried in her hands. It couldn't touch what she carried by heart.
Section twenty-four of the Diamond Sutra sets those two kinds of keeping side by side, and it doesn't hold back on the size of the pile.

teach.b: First, the heap. Someone piles up the seven precious things, gold, silver and the rest, in heaps as high as all the Sumeru mountains in a vast world system, and gives them all away.
Sumeru, in Buddhist cosmology, is the great mountain at the center of a world, so this is a gift the size of a mountain range, made of treasure.
Second, the four lines. Someone else takes this teaching of the perfection of wisdom, even just four lines of it, keeps it, recites it, and explains it to others. That's all.
The merit of the mountain of jewels, the Buddha says, is not a hundredth part of the merit of the four lines. Not the tiniest share, not any fraction you could name or compare.
The sutra pushes the numbers until numbers give up.
Fourth, why. We've heard this comparison before, but today's picture makes the reason plain. Jewels are given once, and then they're gone, or lost, or fought over.
Four lines kept by heart travel with a person through sleepless nights and hospital waiting rooms, and when they're explained to someone else, nobody has less.
All week the sutra has been taking things away: no grasping the mind, no merit to own, no perfect body, nothing to teach, nothing gained, no high or low.
Then it hands back something small enough to carry anywhere: a few lines, by heart.

how: In some Mahayana communities people memorize and chant verses of the Diamond Sutra, and teach them to others, which the sutra names as a way of keeping it.

o: mountains of treasure, worth less than four lines shared
the jewels piled on a shrine on festival days
a heavenly palace built of gold and precious stones

games.q: less than four lines: tap the pairs.
p: the great mountain at a world's center
the mountain of jewels, by comparison

s: the sutra says a mountain of jewels and four lines are about equal in merit
the jewels are not a hundredth part, nor any fraction that can be named.
section 24 counts four lines that are kept, recited and explained to others
even just four lines of this teaching of wisdom.
the heap in section 24 is as high as all the Sumeru mountains in a world system
a gift of seven precious things on the scale of a mountain range.

games.q: you can give away jewels heaped as high as the Sumeru mountains, or keep four lines of this teaching and explain them to someone. by section 24, which is the greater merit?
games.why: the jewels aren't a hundredth part of it, the Buddha says, nor any part that numbers or comparisons can reach.

practice: Here are four of this week's lines: can't be grasped, so-called merit, not the least thing, no high, no low.
Say one silently on each out-breath, in order, then try them again without help; if one slips, wait a breath and let it come back on its own, and if it doesn't, that's all right.
Go round again, a little slower, until they're yours to carry without a page.

wordCard.voice: Heaps of jewels. In section twenty-four, treasure piled as high as mountains gives less merit than keeping and sharing four lines of this teaching. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: jewel, precious thing; the seven precious things are sapta ratna.

carryVoice: Your line: less than four lines. A mountain of jewels weighs less than a verse you know by heart. That's the week, by heart.
